You have attempted this same task before and did not succeed. These are the plans you wrote after those attempts.
Trial #1: New plan: My previous attempt failed because I relied solely on semantic plausibility (feedback is usually about the recipient) without considering the specific linguistic constraints or potential ambiguity of the sentence structure. In the sentence "The supervisor gave the employee feedback on his stellar performance," while it is common for feedback to be about the employee, the pronoun "his" is grammatically ambiguous as it could technically refer to either the supervisor or the employee without further context. I incorrectly assumed a single logical answer (B) when the correct classification for this type of Winograd Schema challenge, given the lack of disambiguating context, is often (C) Ambiguous. Next time, I will strictly evaluate if the sentence structure *forces* a specific antecedent or if multiple interpretations are grammatically valid. If the pronoun could refer to either noun phrase without creating a contradiction, I will select "Ambiguous" rather than guessing based on real-world probability.

New plan: My previous attempt failed because I over-analyzed the semantic probability of "feedback" scenarios and incorrectly concluded the sentence was ambiguous, whereas the provided examples demonstrate a pattern of resolving pronouns based on the most logical real-world interpretation of the action. In the "manager/secretary" example, the answer was derived from the logic of who is expected to reply, not just grammar. Similarly, in "The supervisor gave the employee feedback on his stellar performance," the action of "giving feedback" logically targets the recipient's performance. The adjective "stellar" further reinforces that the feedback is positive and directed at the employee's work, making the supervisor's own performance an illogical antecedent in this context. Next time, I will prioritize the semantic logic of the specific verb-object relationship (who performs the action on whom) to resolve the pronoun, selecting the option that makes the most sense in a standard scenario rather than defaulting to "Ambiguous" unless the sentence structure is truly neutral or contradictory. I will select (B) as the answer.
